Triggers on phrases like "replay <feature>", "walk me through how X was built", "show me the journey of", "step me through how Y was implemented", and "replay the last week"

- entire:session-to-skill: Use when the user wants to turn one or more Entire-tracked sessions, checkpoints, or repeated agent workflows into a reusable agent skill.
- entire:teach: Use when a developer wants a topic-focused guided lesson built from canonical checkpoints, not a whole-repo overview. Triggers on phrases like "teach me <topic>", "teach me how this repo handles", "how does <topic> work in this repo", "give me a lesson on", "school me on", and "I need to learn about"
- entire:using-entire: Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
- entire:what-happened: Explain why code looks the way it does by tracing the latest change for a file range or pasted snippet through `git blame` and deduplicated `entire explain` lookups. Use when the user asks what happened, says "tell me why" about a code block, is confused about a section of code, asks "wtf is going on", "why is this like this", "why was this changed", or wants provenance for a specific file block.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content:
1	# DevDesk Backlog
2	
3	**Last Updated:** 2026-08-03
4	
5	Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
6	Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
7	(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
8	rather than carried over.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 1. Known defects
13	
14	**Three open**, all in the registry browser and all found while reviewing the
15	design for §3.8 rather than by a test; see [§1.3](#13-open). D1–D11 are fixed;
16	§1.1 records what each was and why the chosen fix was the right one.
17	
18	The five that stayed open longest — D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 — were parked not
19	because they were hard but because each altered something the user already saw,
20	so they needed a deliberate call rather than a drive-by fix. All five were then
21	decided together and fixed in one pass; see [§1.2](#12-the-five-parked-defects).
22	
23	### 1.1 Fixed
24	
25	**The command line took focus from the render path.** Found in phase 5.
26	`renderHeader` called `a.commandInput.Focus()` whenever `commandMode` was set —
27	a mutation inside `View()`, which Rule 110 makes read-only. A
28	`bubbles/textinput` drops every key it receives while blurred, so the command
29	line only accepted typing because a render happened to have run first. Focus is
30	now taken in `enterCommandMode` and released alongside the existing `Blur()`
31	calls on the way out. In production the ordering held, so nothing was visibly
32	broken; the coupling surfaced the moment a test drove the router without
33	rendering, and the same latent bug would bite anyone reordering the loop.
34	
35	**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
36	phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.
37	
38	The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
39	the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
40	was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
41	The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
42	without documenting it at all.
43	
44	The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
45	where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
46	stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.
47	
48	`explorer` made it four in a row, though only just: every key was documented
49	except `/`. The check caught it on its first run.
50	
51	`security` broke the streak — its help documents every key its header
52	advertises, across all four states.
53	
54	`oci_resources` then produced the worst instance, in phase 4. The Networks and
55	Volumes tabs documented `n` for a binding that has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111
56	renamed it — the same drift `status` and `workspaces` carried — but the **whole
57	Registries tab was undocumented**: `ctrl+n`, `e`, `l` and `L` appeared nowhere,
58	so four actions on a tab were reachable only by guessing.
59	
60	That view needed one adjustment to the check: its help qualifies most keys with
61	the tab they belong to (`enter (Images)`, `ctrl+n (Networks)`), so the
62	parenthetical comes off before matching. That convention is worth keeping — with
63	four tabs sharing a keymap, an unqualified `enter` would be ambiguous.
64	
65	So the pattern across five views: the drift is a Rule 111 rename the help did
66	not follow, plus whole surfaces added later and never documented at all.
67	
68	All five are fixed, and every view in `internal/ui` now asserts that each key
69	`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
70	have caught the drift when it was introduced.
71	
72	**The explorer acted on a different row than the one highlighted.** Found in
73	phase 3, and the most serious defect the coverage work has turned up.
74	
75	`handleKeyMsg` resolved the cursor against `sortedItems(currentItems())` — the
76	unfiltered list — while the table was built from the filtered one. With a filter
77	active the two indices disagree, so `ctrl+d`, `p`, `→` and `ctrl+w` all acted on
78	whatever happened to sit at that index in the *unfiltered* list. Filtering to a
79	single project and pressing `ctrl+d` scheduled a different group for deletion.
80	`GetShortcuts` had it too, so even the advertised `ctrl+w` keyed off the wrong
81	node.
82	
83	Both now go through `visibleItems()`, the single list `updateTableRows` builds
84	from. Pinned by `TestActionsResolveTheRowTheUserCanSee`, which filters to a row
85	that sits at a different index in each list — the fixtures were chosen so the
86	two cannot coincide.
87	
88	**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
89	clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
90	fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
91	highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
92	until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.
93	
94	The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
95	change; workspaces had no equivalent. **`explorer` had it too**, and only on the
96	filter path — its drill-down was already safe because it calls `GotoTop()`.
97	Fixed the same way.
98	
99	**Two tabs reported nothing when Docker was down.** Found in phase 4.
100	`handleImagesList` has always set a footer message on failure;
101	`handleNetworksList` and `handleVolumesList` only logged, so with the daemon
102	stopped those two tabs showed an empty table — indistinguishable from "you have
103	no networks". Both now match their sibling.
104	
105	**The Registries tab opened empty.** `switchTab` focused the table and fired the
106	`docker login` status check, but never called `updateRegistryTable()` — so the
107	tab stayed blank until an asynchronous Docker call answered, even though the
108	registries come from the config file and were available immediately.
109	
110	**A search counter with no floor.** `RegistryBrowser.AddRegistryTags`
111	decremented `pendingSearches` unconditionally. A duplicate or late response drove
112	it negative, and the *next* search then started from that base: `IsSearching()`
113	stayed false while requests were genuinely in flight, so the spinner never
114	showed. Floored at zero.
115	
116	**Footer messages with no timer.** `explorer.handleDeleteComplete` set
117	`footerError` and returned `nil`, so a failed delete left "Delete failed — check
118	logs" on screen until something else overwrote it. Rule 128 caps footer messages
119	at three seconds, and the same file's `BrowserOpenedMsg` handler already did it
120	correctly. Now returns `clearFooterErrorCmd()`.
121	
122	The security view had it worse: **Rule 128 was not honoured anywhere in it.**
123	`statusMessage` was set in three places — "Added x to .gitleaksignore", "Failed
124	to ignore secret", "No references available" — and there was no clear timer in
125	the package at all, so whichever happened last stayed on screen until a tab
126	switch happened to reset it. `clearStatusCmd` / `clearStatusMsg` added and all
127	three wired, pinned by `TestFooterMessagesExpire`.
128	
129	**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
130	"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
131	unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
132	independent defects with no shared code.
133	
134	`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
135	normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
136	Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
137	`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
138	silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
139	(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
140	first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
141	that treats it as one.
142	
143	The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
144	`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
145	navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
146	line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
147	confusing than one that is plainly not there.
148	
149	The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
150	cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
151	was guarding.
152	
153	Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
154	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
155	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
156	confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
157	`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
158	alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.
159	
160	**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
161	looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
162	fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.
163	
164	Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
165	`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
166	the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
167	terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
168	ones.
169	
170	A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
171	in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
172	Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
173	gone.
174	
175	A **sixth site** closed the family out, in the last package of phase 3:
176	`parseVersion` in `internal/ui/security` truncated its fallback with
177	`result[:15]`. Version strings are ASCII in practice, so this was the
178	lowest-risk of the six — but it is the same pattern, and it is now
179	`theme.TruncateWidth`. Grepping for `[:` on strings across `internal/ui` now
180	returns nothing but slice indexing.
181	
182	The same function had a second defect: it scanned for the version number by
183	taking the first whitespace-separated token starting with `v`, so
184	`gitleaks version 8.18.2` reported its version as **"version"**. A leading `v`
185	now only counts when a digit follows it.
186	
187	A **fifth site** turned up during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
188	`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
189	results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
190	could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
191	`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
192	Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.
193	
194	The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
195	(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
196	`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).
197	
198	One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
199	`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
200	so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
201	theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.
202	
203	**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
204	planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.
205	
206	The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
207	credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
208	unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
209	credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
210	same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
211	won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
212	after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
213	strips the path before the helper is ever called.
214	
215	**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
216	the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
217	change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
218	`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.
219	
220	Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
221	path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
222	contexts anyway.
223	
224	Two smaller defects went with it:
225	
226	- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
227	  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
228	  hang indefinitely.
229	- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
230	  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
231	  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
232	  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.
233	
234	`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
235	than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
236	`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
237	common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
238	`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
239	`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.
240	
241	### 1.2 The five parked defects
242	
243	D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 were each recorded rather than fixed on discovery,
244	because each changed something the user already saw. They were decided together
245	and fixed in one pass. Three of the five had a test written to fail *on the
246	fix*, and all three did.
247	
248	**D4 — `tab` navigated the delete confirmation.** Rule 135 reserves `tab` for
249	switching tabs and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively; the modal
250	had it exactly inverted, cycling on `tab` and clamping on `↑ / ↓`. `↑ / ↓` now
251	cycle, which is what keeps every control reachable in one direction, and the
252	`tab` cases are gone. The explorer no longer advertises "tab Navigate" while the
253	modal is open, and `↑↓` is not advertised in its place — Rule 138 calls it
254	obvious. The permanent variant still skips its locked checkbox, so cycling there
255	toggles between the two buttons.
256	
257	**D8 — write-only CRUD flags.** `creating`, `editing` and `confirming` were
258	assigned in five places and read in none, and `ComponentFormCancelledMsg` — the
259	only thing that would have reset two of them — could never be sent. Deleted, all
260	of it. Nothing else changed: the phase 2 tests had deliberately asserted on
261	`componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags, which is what made
262	this safe a phase later.
263	
264	**D9 — the containers list opened Z→A.** `New()` set neither `sortColumn` nor
265	`sortAsc`, so both took their zero value. Both are now set explicitly, so the
266	default is stated rather than inherited. `TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending`
267	became `TestDefaultSortIsNameAscending`, and the cycle test walks forward from
268	ascending. The `loadedModel` helper still sets the sort itself even though it
269	now matches the constructor: those tests should say which order they rely on.
270	
271	**D10 — a registry failure was invisible.** `renderTemplateList` returned early
272	when the field was unfocused and the warning sat below that return, so a form
273	opened after the OCI registry failed offered a Template field reading "none"
274	with nothing to distinguish "the registry is down" from "there are no
275	templates". The warning moved into `renderTemplateWarning` and is appended in
276	both branches — it explains why the list is empty, so it belongs wherever the
277	list is.
278	
279	**D11 — CRITICAL and HIGH rendered identically.** `getSeverityStyle` composed
280	CRITICAL by hand as `ColorError` + `Bold`, which is byte-for-byte the
281	`theme.StatusErrorStyle` it returned for HIGH. The palette moved to
282	`theme.SeverityTextStyle`, next to the `TableStylesForSeverity` it draws from,
283	and the view delegates (Rule 102). An unrecognised severity now falls back to
284	the info colour rather than to `DimStyle`, so it is still legible.
285	
286	The pattern worth keeping: when a defect is recorded rather than fixed, write
287	the test **inverted** — asserting the current behaviour and saying so. D9, D10
288	and D11 each had one, and each failed the moment the fix landed, which is how
289	the stale test and the stale backlog entry got found together.
290	
291	### 1.3 Open
292	
293	D12–D14 sit in `internal/ui/oci_resources` and are cheap on their own, but
294	§3.8 rewrites the code path each of them lives in. Fix them **as part of** that
295	work rather than ahead of it, and write each one's test inverted first, per the
296	pattern above.
297	
298	D15–D19 were found by the phase 5 router pass and are unrelated to §3.8. Each
299	has an inverted test asserting the current behaviour, named in its entry.
300	
301	**D12 — `AuthEnabled` has no effect on browse or discovery.** The flag is
302	honoured in exactly three places: the `docker login` fired on form submit, the
303	`Logged` column, and the URL list `registryLoginStatusCmd` checks. Neither code
304	path that actually talks to a registry consults it. `submitSearch`
305	(`browser_keys.go:142`) calls `docker.GetStoredCreds(credURL)`
306	unconditionally and hands the result to `searchRegistryTagsCmd`;
307	`detectRegistryGroupCmd` (`commands.go:563`) does the same before calling into
308	`registrymgr`. A registry the user has marked as needing no authentication will
309	still have the host's stored credentials sent to it whenever any other registry
310	on that host has been logged into — which, given that Docker keys credentials by
311	host, is the normal case for a Nexus instance. This is the defect the
312	`anonymous` mode in §3.8 exists to make expressible; today there is no way to
313	say "do not send credentials here" at all.
314	
315	**D13 — the browser cannot be dismissed while it is resolving.**
316	`handleKeyMsg` returns `nil` for every key in `browserStateResolving`
317	(`browser_keys.go:70`), `esc` included, and that state is entered
318	unconditionally on open whenever any registry is configured. The detections run
319	concurrently with an 8 s timeout each, so the wedge is bounded at roughly eight
320	seconds — but it is eight seconds during which the application ignores the user,
321	on a screen they may have opened by mistake. §3.8 removes the state rather than
322	the symptom: with members read from config and cache, there is nothing to
323	resolve and the form renders immediately.
324	
325	A smaller thing in the same handler, not worth its own entry:
326	`HandleGroupDetected` matches the incoming result against `reg.URL`, so two
327	registries configured with the same URL collide and the second result overwrites
328	the first. The slug introduced in §3.8 is the natural key to match on instead.
329	
330	**D14 — the registry filter shows a raw URL for group members.**
331	`registryFilterLabel()` (`browser_tags.go:63`) resolves the active filter by
332	searching `b.registries`, which holds only the configured top-level entries.
333	Discovered members are not in that list, so filtering to one falls through to
334	returning `b.registryFilter` — the full synthesised URL — where every other row
335	in the same view shows a short alias. The fix follows from §3.8 rather than
336	preceding it: once members are persisted they are resolvable, and the filter
337	gains a group level at the same time.
338	
339	**D15 — `esc` never reaches a view that is not editing.** `handleKeyMsg`
340	(`keys.go`) answers `esc` itself through `maybeQuitCommandMode`, which forwards
341	the key only when the view reports `InEditMode()`. Every other time the router
342	consumes it and returns a resize. The explorer's `esc` → `handleDrillUp`
343	(`update.go:157`) is therefore dead code: only `←` and `h` drill up, though
344	Rule 111 lists `esc` as the third way. The explorer's own unit tests pass
345	because they drive the model directly, bypassing the router — this is precisely
346	the class of defect router tests exist to catch.
347	
348	The security view already works around it: `InEditMode()` there is documented as
349	*"returns true when the view needs to handle ESC key"*, which overloads a
350	predicate about focused fields into a predicate about key ownership. The fix is
351	to give `esc` the same shape as every other key — forward it to the view first
352	and let the router act only if the view did not — but that changes behaviour in
353	every view at once, so it wants its own commit and a pass over each view's esc
354	handling. Inverted test:
355	`TestEscIsSwallowedForAViewThatIsNotEditing` (`router_test.go`).
356	
357	**D16 — `:netdiag` is documented but not accepted.** `CLAUDE.md` lists
358	"`netdiag` or `net`", the view is named `netdiag` throughout, and the directory
359	is `internal/ui/netdiag` — but `viewMap` in `parser.go` has only `"net"`.
360	`:netdiag` parses to `CommandUnknown`, which leaves the command line open with
361	no diagnostic. One map entry. Covered by the comment on the `net` row in
362	`TestEveryNamedViewCanBeReached` (`command_line_test.go`).
363	
364	**D17 — the completion catalogue is a subset of the parser.**
365	`buildCommands()` (`completion.go`) lists eight full commands; the parser
366	accepts fourteen views plus aliases. `gitlab-explorer`, `workspaces`,
367	`security` and `net` all work when typed in full but cannot be tab-completed,
368	and nothing keeps the two lists in step. The parser's `viewMap` is the natural
369	single source — the catalogue should be derived from it rather than restated.
370	Worth doing with D16, which is the same drift.
371	
372	**D18 — the header overflows a narrow window.** `buildShortcutLines`
373	(`app_header.go:202`) intends to clip the shortcut block to its column —
374	`// Truncate if wider than col2Width` — but calls `theme.PadWithBg`, which
375	returns the content untouched when it is already at or past the target. Below
376	roughly 100 columns the header therefore renders wider than the window and
377	wraps: at width 80 with twelve shortcuts every header row comes out 95 wide.
378	The fix is `lipgloss.NewStyle().MaxWidth(col2Width)`, which truncates without
379	cutting an escape sequence in half — the hazard Rule 122 is about. Inverted
380	test: `TestANarrowHeaderOverflowsTheWindow` (`header_test.go`).
381	
382	**D19 — the Trivy command shown is not the one run.** `GetTrivyCommand` exists
383	to display what will be executed, and rebuilds the argument list by hand from
384	the same inputs as `RunTrivy`. The two have drifted: `RunTrivy` takes
385	`ignoreEOL` and appends `--ignore-status end_of_life`; `GetTrivyCommand` does
386	not take the parameter at all. A user copying the logged command gets different
387	results from the scan they just watched. `RunTrivyMisconfig` and `GenerateSBOM`
388	have no display counterpart at all, so their commands are never shown.
389	
390	The fix is not to add the missing flag but to remove the duplication: extract
391	one pure `trivyArgs(...)` builder returning the binary name and its arguments,
392	and have `RunTrivy` turn it into an `exec.Cmd` while `GetTrivyCommand` joins it
393	into a string. Same for gitleaks. This is planned as the split step of phase 5
394	for `internal/scan`, since it is also what makes the argument surface testable.

655	### Race detector cannot run locally
656	
657	`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
658	it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
659	concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.
660	
661	**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
662	every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
663	run reported no data race across all 17 packages.
664	
665	That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
666	tests actually execute, and coverage is 65.2 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
667	paths — most of the view layer — remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so
668	this is an argument for the coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.
669	Phase 2 puts the first full view state machine under the detector.
670	
671	Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
672	avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.

753	**The command surface is already duplicated four times, and already drifting.**
754	
755	| Location | Role |
756	|---|---|
757	| `parser.go:78` `viewMap` | `ParseCommand()` — the authoritative one |
758	| `parser.go:120` `commands` | `Parse()`, legacy, duplicates the above |
759	| `parser.go:155` `GetAliases()` | feeds completion |
760	| `completion.go:47` `buildCommands` | a fourth hardcoded list, **stale today** |
761	
762	`buildCommands` offers `gitlab-auth` but not `gitlab-explorer`, and omits
763	`workspaces`, `security` and `net` entirely — so those commands work but are
764	never suggested. Adding a forge dimension to four unsynchronised tables
765	guarantees the drift gets worse. **Collapsing them to one source table is a
766	prerequisite**, and it is worth doing on its own: it fixes the stale completion
767	list today, independently of GitHub.
768	
769	#### Model mismatches to settle before coding
770	
771	These are not implementation details; they decide what the abstraction can even
772	promise.
773	
774	- **Nesting — settled.** The explorer is a tree of groups → subgroups →
775	  projects. GitHub has no nested groups, but it does have **organisations**, and
776	  a user can belong to several. Flattening everything to one level was
777	  considered and rejected: someone in five orgs would get a wall of repositories
778	  with no way to tell them apart by owner. The abstraction therefore **declares
779	  its depth** — `MaxDepth: 1` for GitHub (orgs at level 1, repositories at level
780	  2), unbounded for GitLab. This costs nothing in the UI: the drill-down already
781	  handles two levels, and a user with no organisation simply sees a flat list.
782	- **Deletion.** `DeleteGroup` / `DeleteProject` implement GitLab's two-step
783	  permanent delete (schedule, then purge under the renamed
784	  `-deletion_scheduled-<id>` path). GitHub deletes immediately and has no
785	  equivalent, so the "permanent" checkbox is meaningless there. The `locked`
786	  flag added in §1.1 is the hook for that: a GitHub backend would set it and
787	  leave the box out of reach, as the already-scheduled GitLab case does.
788	- **Dashboard counters.** `FetchDashboardStats` reads `X-Total` from five list
789	  endpoints. GitHub has no equivalent header for these; the counts come from the
790	  search API (`search/issues?q=is:open+is:pr+assignee:@me`), with different rate
791	  limits and semantics.
792	- **Vocabulary.** Group/project/merge request vs organisation/repository/pull
793	  request. The UI must pick per-backend labels or a neutral vocabulary; Rule 129
794	  applies either way.
795	
796	#### Settled: vocabulary, commands and forge selection
797	
798	The organising distinction, which the mismatches above blur: the two forges
799	differ in **words** and in **shapes**, and only the first is a presentation
800	problem.
801	
802	| Difference | Kind | Handled by |
803	|---|---|---|
804	| "Group" vs "Organization" | word | vocabulary table |
805	| "Merge Request" vs "Pull Request" | word | vocabulary table |
806	| Token label, placeholder, help URL | word | vocabulary table |
807	| Icon and display name | word | vocabulary table |
808	| Nested namespaces | **shape** | declared depth (above) |
809	| Visibility set — 3 values vs 2 | **shape** | forge-supplied option list |
810	| Role model — int levels vs strings | **shape** | backend returns a humanised role |
811	| Two-step permanent delete | **shape** | the `locked` flag, §1.1 |
812	| Dashboard counters | **shape** | different endpoints, above |
813	
814	Words are cheap and settle in one pass. Shapes are the actual work, and neither
815	neutral nor per-forge wording helps with them. Keeping the two apart is what
816	stops the vocabulary layer from quietly growing conditionals.
817	
818	**Vocabulary is per-forge, not neutral.** A GitLab user says *group*, a GitHub
819	user says *repository*; "namespace" is a third language nobody speaks, and it
820	makes the application read as an abstraction layer rather than a tool. The
821	wording lives in a single `Vocabulary` value per forge — name, icon, namespace
822	singular/plural, repository, change-request, token label and placeholder, help
823	URL, visibility set, role names — resolved once from the active context and
824	carried on `shared.State`, which every view already receives.
825	
826	The rule that keeps it maintainable: **no view interpolates a forge name into a
827	string literal.** That is enforceable the way this project already pins
828	invariants — a test grepping `internal/ui` for `"GitLab"` / `"GitHub"`, on the
829	model of the existing check that every key in `GetShortcuts()` appears in
830	`GetHelpContent()`.
831	
832	Sites to move, none of them subtle:
833	
834	| Location | Literal |
835	|---|---|
836	| `explorer/view.go:342` | `IconGitlab + " GitLab Explorer"` |
837	| `explorer/view.go:258` | `"GitLab not authenticated … with :gitlab-auth (or :gla)"` — name **and** command |
838	| `explorer/view.go:267` | `"No groups found … any GitLab groups."` |
839	| `explorer/view.go:81` | `"Loading GitLab groups..."` |
840	| `explorer/view.go:210` | `nodeTypeLabel()` → `"Group"` / `"Project"` |
841	| `components/creation_form.go:26` | `resourceTypes = []string{"Group", "Project"}` |
842	| `auth/view.go:46` | `IconUser + " Gitlab Authentication"` — wrong icon *and* wrong casing next to the explorer's |
843	| `auth/view.go:132,140` | `"GitLab URL"`, `"Personal Access Token"` |
844	| `auth/view.go:81` | help text asserting the token starts with `glpat-` |
845	| `dashboard/view.go:80,85` | `IconGitlab + " GitLab"`, `"Authenticate with :gitlab-auth"` |
846	| `dashboard/view.go:104` | `"Merge Requests:"` |
847	
848	Two of these are shapes wearing a word's clothes. `AccessLevelName()`
849	(`tree.go:52`) maps GitLab's numeric levels to Owner/Maintainer/…; GitHub uses
850	`admin`/`maintain`/`push`/`triage`/`pull`, which do not align one-to-one — so the
851	**backend returns an already-humanised role string** rather than an integer the
852	UI translates. And `internal` visibility does not exist on GitHub.com, so
853	`CreationForm`'s three hardcoded values have to come from the forge. Nothing to
854	undo for the token prefix: `glpat-` appears only in help text, never validated.
855	
856	**Routing identity is forge-neutral; only aliases and titles vary.** `ViewType`
857	is a map key in `a.views` and a `switch` case in `app.go:1480,1496`, so it stays
858	stable — otherwise every new forge touches the router. Canonical names become
859	neutral (`explorer` is already an alias and becomes the name; `auth` for the
860	other), and `gitlab-auth` / `gla` **and** `github-auth` / `gha` all parse, to the
861	same view.
862	
863	Deliberately permissive: there is only one authentication view, so `gla` typed
864	in a GitHub context should go there rather than fail. Punishing muscle memory
865	buys nothing. **The filtering happens in completion, not in parsing** — `gla`
866	always works, but is never *suggested* while the active forge is GitHub. That
867	split is what makes it feel fluid without breaking anything existing.
868	
869	Messages that quote a command (`explorer/view.go:258`,
870	`dashboard/view.go:85`) must quote the active forge's spelling; once the
871	vocabulary is centralised that is one more field on the same struct.
872	
873	**Forge selection: detect, and let the user take it back.** URL sniffing alone is
874	unreliable — `github.com` and `gitlab.com` are trivial, but self-hosted is the
875	case that matters and `git.acme.com` could be either. Probing (`/api/v4/version`
876	vs `/api/v3/`) costs a round-trip and fails on instances that require auth on
877	those endpoints. A mandatory picker alone is friction on the two most common
878	cases, where the URL is unambiguous. So:
879	
880	- The forge is **field 0** of the auth form, above the URL. It governs the URL
881	  placeholder, the token placeholder and label, and the scope help — putting it
882	  first is what lets everything below it reconfigure live.
883	- It is a **cycle field** (`←` / `→`, Rule 132), pre-filled by host detection.
884	- Detection re-runs as the URL is typed, **but only while the user has not
885	  touched the forge field** — a dirty flag. Without it, detection overwrites an
886	  explicit choice, which is the difference between helpful and possessive.
887	- The token prefix (`glpat-` vs `ghp_` / `github_pat_`) is a second signal used
888	  to **warn**, never to switch: by then the user has already chosen above.
889	- **Once authentication succeeds the forge is frozen for that context**, per the
890	  one-forge-per-context decision. Changing it requires an explicit logout, or a
891	  new context. Before a successful login it stays freely editable.
892	
893	This makes the auth form mix a cycle field with the radio buttons it uses for
894	the save options (`auth/view.go:146`) — themselves a closed two-value set, so
895	the form was already at odds with Rule 132. **Settled in §3.9**: those radios are
896	deleted outright, along with the choice they present, so the form is left with a
897	cycle field and nothing else.
898	
899	#### Open decision: Go SDKs or the `gh` / `glab` CLIs
900	
901	Worth deciding before any code is written, because it determines whether the
902	package needs a seam.
903	
904	Arguments for the CLIs:
905	
906	- Authentication is already solved, including OAuth device flow, self-hosted
907	  hosts and token storage. DevDesk's own credential handling could shrink — and
908	  it has already proven fragile (see §1.1).
909	- `gh api` and `glab api` are raw REST/GraphQL passthroughs, so no SDK is needed
910	  for coverage of endpoints the abstraction does not model.
911	- No SDK version churn to track for two forges.
912	
913	Arguments against:
914	
915	- **Per-context isolation conflicts with how these tools store auth.** Both keep
916	  global per-host state (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`). DevDesk contexts want
917	  *different tokens for the same host*. Driving `gh auth switch` from the TUI
918	  would mutate the user's global CLI state — the exact mistake avoided in §1.1 by
919	  scoping `credential.useHttpPath` to the invocation. The clean route is
920	  `GH_TOKEN` / `GITLAB_TOKEN` per invocation, but then DevDesk still owns the
921	  tokens and the main benefit is gone.
922	- **Two more hard dependencies.** Today DevDesk needs `git`, and `docker` only
923	  for the features that use it. Requiring `gh` and `glab` for the core forge
924	  feature is a real setup-friction regression.
925	- **Cost per call.** A process spawn per request, against a reused HTTP
926	  connection today. The dashboard alone issues five calls, and the explorer
927	  paginates.
928	- **Testability regresses.** `internal/gitlab` reaches 100 % with no seam,
929	  because the SDK takes a base URL that an `httptest` server can stand in for.
930	  Shelling out would put it back in the position `internal/docker` was in, needing
931	  a manufactured seam — and stubbed CLI output encodes assumptions about the tool
932	  rather than testing against it.
933	
934	**Current recommendation:** keep Go SDKs (go-gitlab, go-github) for the API
935	surface, and use the CLIs only as an *optional* token source — when a context has
936	no token, offer to read one from `gh auth token --hostname <host>` or
937	`glab auth status`. That takes the convenience without the coupling. Recorded as
938	a recommendation, not a decision.
939	
940	#### Sketch of the work
941	
942	0. Collapse the four command tables into one source, and let `Parse`,
943	   `GetAliases` and `buildCommands` derive from it. Independent of everything
944	   else, and it fixes the stale completion list today.
945	1. Define a `forge` abstraction from what the code actually consumes: current
946	   user, namespace tree, create/delete namespace and repository, initial commit,
947	   dashboard counters, clone URL. It also declares its **shape** — depth,
948	   visibility set, humanised roles — not just its data.
949	2. Replace `shared.State.GitLabClient` with that interface, and switch the
950	   authenticated-or-not branches to `IsAuthenticated` while passing through.
951	   This is the change the other 65 call sites follow from.
952	3. Generalise `GitLabConfig` into a per-context forge config carrying a
953	   `type: gitlab | github` discriminator, and migrate existing config files.
954	4. Extract the `Vocabulary` table and move every literal in the table above onto
955	   it, with the grep test that keeps them from coming back. Doable against
956	   GitLab alone, before any GitHub code exists — which is what makes it a
957	   refactor rather than a rewrite.
958	5. Implement the GitLab backend by moving the existing code behind the
959	   interface — behaviour-preserving, and covered by the tests §2 phase 5 adds.
960	6. Implement the GitHub backend.
961	7. Rename the views and commands, keeping `gla` / `gle` as aliases so muscle
962	   memory survives, and make completion forge-aware.
963	
964	Steps 0 and 4 stand alone and improve the code with no GitHub in sight. Steps
965	1–5 are a refactor of working code with tests already in place, and they are
966	what makes step 6 tractable.
967	
968	### 3.7 Command mode from inside a text field — **done**
969	
970	`alt+:` now opens the command line from anywhere, including a focused text
971	input. A bare `:` keeps its old, conditional behaviour, so muscle memory
972	survives.
973	
974	The problem: `handleKeyMsg` routed `:` through `maybeEnterInCommandMode`, which
975	asked the view whether it was in edit mode (`FormView.InEditMode()`) and, if it
976	was, forwarded the keystroke to the active input. Command mode was therefore
977	unreachable from any form, filter box or search field — most of the application.
978	
979	The security view is the case that settles it. `InEditMode()` is true there for
980	the target path, Trivy server and Gitleaks config fields, and the Trivy server
981	placeholder is `https://trivy-server:4954` — the field has to accept **two**
982	colons to hold a valid value. Forwarding `:` to the input is not a bug; it is
983	the only correct behaviour, which is precisely why `:` cannot be the
984	authoritative key. The only way in was to move focus to a control that takes no
985	text and press `:` there, so reachability depended on which widget was focused
986	and nothing said so.
987	
988	It was worse in `StateScanning`, `StateResults`, `StateDetails` and while a
989	confirm modal is open: `InEditMode()` is true and there is no field to move
990	focus to. `:` was forwarded to the view, which has no `case` for it — no view in
991	the application handles `:` itself — and dropped silently.
992	
993	#### Why `alt+`, not `ctrl+`
994	
995	`ctrl+:` cannot be made to work, and this is the note that should stop anyone
996	reintroducing it. A terminal encodes Ctrl by clearing bits, which only covers
997	ASCII `@` through `_` (0x40–0x5F). `:` is 0x3A: Ctrl+: sends a plain `:` or
998	nothing. Reporting it as a distinct key needs the Kitty keyboard protocol or
999	xterm's `modifyOtherKeys`, and bubbletea v1.3.10 implements neither. A
1000	`case "ctrl+:"` would be dead code.
1001	
1002	Alt has no such limit — a terminal sends ESC then the key, and bubbletea reports
1003	that as the key carrying `Alt`. The alternative considered was a free
1004	`ctrl+<letter>` (`b g l p t u v x z` are unused; `ctrl+i m j h [` are Tab, Enter,
1005	LF, Backspace and Esc and must be left alone), which is marginally more portable
1006	but loses the `:` in the gesture.
1007	
1008	#### What shipped
1009	
1010	- `altCommandModeKey` is handled in `handleKeyMsg` **before** the `InEditMode()`
1011	  fork, so no view can claim it. The router sees every `tea.KeyMsg` first, which
1012	  is what makes the binding unconditional.
1013	- `enterCommandMode()` extracted; `maybeEnterInCommandMode` now only answers the
1014	  bare `:`.
1015	- `testutil.Key` understands an `alt+` prefix, building the key with the `Alt`
1016	  modifier rather than the five literal runes `alt+:`. Both round-trip through
1017	  `String()`, but only one is the message the application actually receives.
1018	- Every `GetShortcuts()` and `GetHelpContent()` advertising `:` now advertises
1019	  `alt+:` (Rules 114, 130, 137). The dashboard's Navigation help section carries
1020	  the nuance in prose, so the other eight sites stay one line each.
1021	- The header still renders `:` as the inactive prompt: it is the command line's
1022	  visual marker, not a key legend, and `:` remains valid whenever no field has
1023	  focus.
1024	
1025	Two things the ripple list got wrong, corrected here: `app_test.go:30` is a
1026	layout fixture for `buildShortcutLines`, not an assertion about the binding, so
1027	it was left alone. And `CommandModeView` / `AllowCommandMode` was not merely
1028	made redundant by this change — **it was already dead code**. The router only
1029	consulted it when `InEditMode()` was true, and netdiag's implementation returns
1030	true only on the topology tab, where `InEditMode()` is unconditionally false. It
1031	could never fire. Deleted, along with its one implementation;
1032	`TestCommandModeOnTheTopologyTab` became
1033	`TestTheTopologyTabNeverBlocksCommandMode` and records why.
1034

# DevDesk Backlog

**Last Updated:** 2026-08-03

Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
rather than carried over.

---

## 1. Known defects

**Three open**, all in the registry browser and all found while reviewing the
design for §3.8 rather than by a test; see [§1.3](#13-open). D1–D11 are fixed;
§1.1 records what each was and why the chosen fix was the right one.

The five that stayed open longest — D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 — were parked not
because they were hard but because each altered something the user already saw,
so they needed a deliberate call rather than a drive-by fix. All five were then
decided together and fixed in one pass; see [§1.2](#12-the-five-parked-defects).

### 1.1 Fixed

**The command line took focus from the render path.** Found in phase 5.
`renderHeader` called `a.commandInput.Focus()` whenever `commandMode` was set —
a mutation inside `View()`, which Rule 110 makes read-only. A
`bubbles/textinput` drops every key it receives while blurred, so the command
line only accepted typing because a render happened to have run first. Focus is
now taken in `enterCommandMode` and released alongside the existing `Blur()`
calls on the way out. In production the ordering held, so nothing was visibly
broken; the coupling surfaced the moment a test drove the router without
rendering, and the same latent bug would bite anyone reordering the loop.

**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.

The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
without documenting it at all.

The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.

`explorer` made it four in a row, though only just: every key was documented
except `/`. The check caught it on its first run.

`security` broke the streak — its help documents every key its header
advertises, across all four states.

`oci_resources` then produced the worst instance, in phase 4. The Networks and
Volumes tabs documented `n` for a binding that has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111
renamed it — the same drift `status` and `workspaces` carried — but the **whole
Registries tab was undocumented**: `ctrl+n`, `e`, `l` and `L` appeared nowhere,
so four actions on a tab were reachable only by guessing.

That view needed one adjustment to the check: its help qualifies most keys with
the tab they belong to (`enter (Images)`, `ctrl+n (Networks)`), so the
parenthetical comes off before matching. That convention is worth keeping — with
four tabs sharing a keymap, an unqualified `enter` would be ambiguous.

So the pattern across five views: the drift is a Rule 111 rename the help did
not follow, plus whole surfaces added later and never documented at all.

All five are fixed, and every view in `internal/ui` now asserts that each key
`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
have caught the drift when it was introduced.

**The explorer acted on a different row than the one highlighted.** Found in
phase 3, and the most serious defect the coverage work has turned up.

`handleKeyMsg` resolved the cursor against `sortedItems(currentItems())` — the
unfiltered list — while the table was built from the filtered one. With a filter
active the two indices disagree, so `ctrl+d`, `p`, `→` and `ctrl+w` all acted on
whatever happened to sit at that index in the *unfiltered* list. Filtering to a
single project and pressing `ctrl+d` scheduled a different group for deletion.
`GetShortcuts` had it too, so even the advertised `ctrl+w` keyed off the wrong
node.

Both now go through `visibleItems()`, the single list `updateTableRows` builds
from. Pinned by `TestActionsResolveTheRowTheUserCanSee`, which filters to a row
that sits at a different index in each list — the fixtures were chosen so the
two cannot coincide.

**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.

The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
change; workspaces had no equivalent. **`explorer` had it too**, and only on the
filter path — its drill-down was already safe because it calls `GotoTop()`.
Fixed the same way.

**Two tabs reported nothing when Docker was down.** Found in phase 4.
`handleImagesList` has always set a footer message on failure;
`handleNetworksList` and `handleVolumesList` only logged, so with the daemon
stopped those two tabs showed an empty table — indistinguishable from "you have
no networks". Both now match their sibling.

**The Registries tab opened empty.** `switchTab` focused the table and fired the
`docker login` status check, but never called `updateRegistryTable()` — so the
tab stayed blank until an asynchronous Docker call answered, even though the
registries come from the config file and were available immediately.

**A search counter with no floor.** `RegistryBrowser.AddRegistryTags`
decremented `pendingSearches` unconditionally. A duplicate or late response drove
it negative, and the *next* search then started from that base: `IsSearching()`
stayed false while requests were genuinely in flight, so the spinner never
showed. Floored at zero.

**Footer messages with no timer.** `explorer.handleDeleteComplete` set
`footerError` and returned `nil`, so a failed delete left "Delete failed — check
logs" on screen until something else overwrote it. Rule 128 caps footer messages
at three seconds, and the same file's `BrowserOpenedMsg` handler already did it
correctly. Now returns `clearFooterErrorCmd()`.

The security view had it worse: **Rule 128 was not honoured anywhere in it.**
`statusMessage` was set in three places — "Added x to .gitleaksignore", "Failed
to ignore secret", "No references available" — and there was no clear timer in
the package at all, so whichever happened last stayed on screen until a tab
switch happened to reset it. `clearStatusCmd` / `clearStatusMsg` added and all
three wired, pinned by `TestFooterMessagesExpire`.

**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
independent defects with no shared code.

`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
that treats it as one.

The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
confusing than one that is plainly not there.

The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
was guarding.

Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.

**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.

Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
ones.

A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
gone.

A **sixth site** closed the family out, in the last package of phase 3:
`parseVersion` in `internal/ui/security` truncated its fallback with
`result[:15]`. Version strings are ASCII in practice, so this was the
lowest-risk of the six — but it is the same pattern, and it is now
`theme.TruncateWidth`. Grepping for `[:` on strings across `internal/ui` now
returns nothing but slice indexing.

The same function had a second defect: it scanned for the version number by
taking the first whitespace-separated token starting with `v`, so
`gitleaks version 8.18.2` reported its version as **"version"**. A leading `v`
now only counts when a digit follows it.

A **fifth site** turned up during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.

The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).

One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.

**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.

The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
strips the path before the helper is ever called.

**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.

Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
contexts anyway.

Two smaller defects went with it:

- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
  hang indefinitely.
- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.

`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.

### 1.2 The five parked defects

D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 were each recorded rather than fixed on discovery,
because each changed something the user already saw. They were decided together
and fixed in one pass. Three of the five had a test written to fail *on the
fix*, and all three did.

**D4 — `tab` navigated the delete confirmation.** Rule 135 reserves `tab` for
switching tabs and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively; the modal
had it exactly inverted, cycling on `tab` and clamping on `↑ / ↓`. `↑ / ↓` now
cycle, which is what keeps every control reachable in one direction, and the
`tab` cases are gone. The explorer no longer advertises "tab Navigate" while the
modal is open, and `↑↓` is not advertised in its place — Rule 138 calls it
obvious. The permanent variant still skips its locked checkbox, so cycling there
toggles between the two buttons.

**D8 — write-only CRUD flags.** `creating`, `editing` and `confirming` were
assigned in five places and read in none, and `ComponentFormCancelledMsg` — the
only thing that would have reset two of them — could never be sent. Deleted, all
of it. Nothing else changed: the phase 2 tests had deliberately asserted on
`componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags, which is what made
this safe a phase later.

**D9 — the containers list opened Z→A.** `New()` set neither `sortColumn` nor
`sortAsc`, so both took their zero value. Both are now set explicitly, so the
default is stated rather than inherited. `TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending`
became `TestDefaultSortIsNameAscending`, and the cycle test walks forward from
ascending. The `loadedModel` helper still sets the sort itself even though it
now matches the constructor: those tests should say which order they rely on.

**D10 — a registry failure was invisible.** `renderTemplateList` returned early
when the field was unfocused and the warning sat below that return, so a form
opened after the OCI registry failed offered a Template field reading "none"
with nothing to distinguish "the registry is down" from "there are no
templates". The warning moved into `renderTemplateWarning` and is appended in
both branches — it explains why the list is empty, so it belongs wherever the
list is.

**D11 — CRITICAL and HIGH rendered identically.** `getSeverityStyle` composed
CRITICAL by hand as `ColorError` + `Bold`, which is byte-for-byte the
`theme.StatusErrorStyle` it returned for HIGH. The palette moved to
`theme.SeverityTextStyle`, next to the `TableStylesForSeverity` it draws from,
and the view delegates (Rule 102). An unrecognised severity now falls back to
the info colour rather than to `DimStyle`, so it is still legible.

The pattern worth keeping: when a defect is recorded rather than fixed, write
the test **inverted** — asserting the current behaviour and saying so. D9, D10
and D11 each had one, and each failed the moment the fix landed, which is how
the stale test and the stale backlog entry got found together.

### 1.3 Open

D12–D14 sit in `internal/ui/oci_resources` and are cheap on their own, but
§3.8 rewrites the code path each of them lives in. Fix them **as part of** that
work rather than ahead of it, and write each one's test inverted first, per the
pattern above.

D15–D19 were found by the phase 5 router pass and are unrelated to §3.8. Each
has an inverted test asserting the current behaviour, named in its entry.

**D12 — `AuthEnabled` has no effect on browse or discovery.** The flag is
honoured in exactly three places: the `docker login` fired on form submit, the
`Logged` column, and the URL list `registryLoginStatusCmd` checks. Neither code
path that actually talks to a registry consults it. `submitSearch`
(`browser_keys.go:142`) calls `docker.GetStoredCreds(credURL)`
unconditionally and hands the result to `searchRegistryTagsCmd`;
`detectRegistryGroupCmd` (`commands.go:563`) does the same before calling into
`registrymgr`. A registry the user has marked as needing no authentication will
still have the host's stored credentials sent to it whenever any other registry
on that host has been logged into — which, given that Docker keys credentials by
host, is the normal case for a Nexus instance. This is the defect the
`anonymous` mode in §3.8 exists to make expressible; today there is no way to
say "do not send credentials here" at all.

**D13 — the browser cannot be dismissed while it is resolving.**
`handleKeyMsg` returns `nil` for every key in `browserStateResolving`
(`browser_keys.go:70`), `esc` included, and that state is entered
unconditionally on open whenever any registry is configured. The detections run
concurrently with an 8 s timeout each, so the wedge is bounded at roughly eight
seconds — but it is eight seconds during which the application ignores the user,
on a screen they may have opened by mistake. §3.8 removes the state rather than
the symptom: with members read from config and cache, there is nothing to
resolve and the form renders immediately.

A smaller thing in the same handler, not worth its own entry:
`HandleGroupDetected` matches the incoming result against `reg.URL`, so two
registries configured with the same URL collide and the second result overwrites
the first. The slug introduced in §3.8 is the natural key to match on instead.

**D14 — the registry filter shows a raw URL for group members.**
`registryFilterLabel()` (`browser_tags.go:63`) resolves the active filter by
searching `b.registries`, which holds only the configured top-level entries.
Discovered members are not in that list, so filtering to one falls through to
returning `b.registryFilter` — the full synthesised URL — where every other row
in the same view shows a short alias. The fix follows from §3.8 rather than
preceding it: once members are persisted they are resolvable, and the filter
gains a group level at the same time.

**D15 — `esc` never reaches a view that is not editing.** `handleKeyMsg`
(`keys.go`) answers `esc` itself through `maybeQuitCommandMode`, which forwards
the key only when the view reports `InEditMode()`. Every other time the router
consumes it and returns a resize. The explorer's `esc` → `handleDrillUp`
(`update.go:157`) is therefore dead code: only `←` and `h` drill up, though
Rule 111 lists `esc` as the third way. The explorer's own unit tests pass
because they drive the model directly, bypassing the router — this is precisely
the class of defect router tests exist to catch.

The security view already works around it: `InEditMode()` there is documented as
*"returns true when the view needs to handle ESC key"*, which overloads a
predicate about focused fields into a predicate about key ownership. The fix is
to give `esc` the same shape as every other key — forward it to the view first
and let the router act only if the view did not — but that changes behaviour in
every view at once, so it wants its own commit and a pass over each view's esc
handling. Inverted test:
`TestEscIsSwallowedForAViewThatIsNotEditing` (`router_test.go`).

**D16 — `:netdiag` is documented but not accepted.** `CLAUDE.md` lists
"`netdiag` or `net`", the view is named `netdiag` throughout, and the directory
is `internal/ui/netdiag` — but `viewMap` in `parser.go` has only `"net"`.
`:netdiag` parses to `CommandUnknown`, which leaves the command line open with
no diagnostic. One map entry. Covered by the comment on the `net` row in
`TestEveryNamedViewCanBeReached` (`command_line_test.go`).

**D17 — the completion catalogue is a subset of the parser.**
`buildCommands()` (`completion.go`) lists eight full commands; the parser
accepts fourteen views plus aliases. `gitlab-explorer`, `workspaces`,
`security` and `net` all work when typed in full but cannot be tab-completed,
and nothing keeps the two lists in step. The parser's `viewMap` is the natural
single source — the catalogue should be derived from it rather than restated.
Worth doing with D16, which is the same drift.

**D18 — the header overflows a narrow window.** `buildShortcutLines`
(`app_header.go:202`) intends to clip the shortcut block to its column —
`// Truncate if wider than col2Width` — but calls `theme.PadWithBg`, which
returns the content untouched when it is already at or past the target. Below
roughly 100 columns the header therefore renders wider than the window and
wraps: at width 80 with twelve shortcuts every header row comes out 95 wide.
The fix is `lipgloss.NewStyle().MaxWidth(col2Width)`, which truncates without
cutting an escape sequence in half — the hazard Rule 122 is about. Inverted
test: `TestANarrowHeaderOverflowsTheWindow` (`header_test.go`).

**D19 — the Trivy command shown is not the one run.** `GetTrivyCommand` exists
to display what will be executed, and rebuilds the argument list by hand from
the same inputs as `RunTrivy`. The two have drifted: `RunTrivy` takes
`ignoreEOL` and appends `--ignore-status end_of_life`; `GetTrivyCommand` does
not take the parameter at all. A user copying the logged command gets different
results from the scan they just watched. `RunTrivyMisconfig` and `GenerateSBOM`
have no display counterpart at all, so their commands are never shown.

The fix is not to add the missing flag but to remove the duplication: extract
one pure `trivyArgs(...)` builder returning the binary name and its arguments,
and have `RunTrivy` turn it into an `exec.Cmd` while `GetTrivyCommand` joins it
into a string. Same for gitleaks. This is planned as the split step of phase 5
for `internal/scan`, since it is also what makes the argument surface testable.

Three constraints the phase surfaced, worth knowing before phases 3–5:

  asserted by looking for the error-selection escape sequence in the rendered

- **`sort.Slice` is not stable**, so fixtures must give every sortable column a

`workspaces` added one technique worth reusing: its filesystem commands
(`createWorkspace`, `deleteEntry`, `renameEntry`, `loadEntries`, `enrichEntry`)
are **executed** rather than asserted on identity, against `t.TempDir()` and a
throwaway git repository. That is what proves the branch, remote and dirty-tree
counters are read correctly; a stub would only prove the stub works. It skips
when `git` is not on `PATH`, like `internal/gitlab` does. Only the Docker- and
desktop-backed commands are left alone.

`explorer` extended that to the API layer, which is why it reaches 91.5 % —
higher than either of the others despite having the largest untestable-looking
surface. The rule that emerged: **execute the command whenever the dependency
can be stood up locally**, and only fall back to asserting on model state when
it cannot.

| Dependency | Treatment |
|---|---|
| GitLab API | executed against `httptest` — the SDK takes a base URL |
| OCI registry | executed against `httptest` |
| git | executed against a seeded repository, skipped without `git` on `PATH` |
| Desktop browser | not executed; the guard branches are driven, the launch is not |

The pull tests are the clearest case: the "GitLab host" is a local directory
holding seeded repositories, so `recursivePull` really clones and really writes
the directory tree. That is what proves the tree mirrors the group hierarchy,
that an existing checkout is skipped rather than clobbered, and that a group
whose children were never browsed is fetched mid-pull. `cloneURL` was extracted
from `pullProject` to make the SSH and HTTPS URL shapes assertable — `gitlab.Clone`
reports only an exit status, so the URL it was handed is not observable through
the error.

The router is where this pass paid for itself. Four of the five defects it found
(D15–D18) are invisible from any single view: `esc` swallowed before it is
forwarded, a documented command the parser rejects, a completion catalogue that
has drifted from the parser, a header that overflows its window. A view's own
tests drive its `Update` directly and so never see the router at all.

### Race detector cannot run locally

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.

**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
run reported no data race across all 17 packages.

That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
tests actually execute, and coverage is 65.2 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
paths — most of the view layer — remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so
this is an argument for the coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.
Phase 2 puts the first full view state machine under the detector.

Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.

## 3. Planned features

Carried over from `todo.md`, except §3.7.

### 3.1 Network diagnostics

- **Port-forwarding manager** — an interactive dashboard to manage port
  redirections to the host machine.

### 3.2 Interactive security remediation

- **Auto-patch assistance** — after a Trivy scan, offer to generate a patch or an

- **Local SAST** — wire security linters (Gitleaks for secrets, IaC linters)
